specStatements.text: Power is defined as the rate at which energy is transferred or the rate at which work is done.
energy transferred, E, in joules, J
work done, W, in joules, J
An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt.

Students should be able to give examples that illustrate the definition of power eg comparing two electric motors that both lift the same weight through the same height but one does it faster than the other.

scopeNotes.statement: power, P, in watts, W / energy transferred, E, in joules, J / time, t, in seconds, s / work done, W, in joules, J
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every quantity is quoted in the unit this section names: power in watts, energy transferred and work done in joules, time in seconds. Kilowatts, megawatts and kilowatt-hours are never used as answers, and where a time is given in minutes the conversion to seconds is part of the question rather than an alternative unit for t.

scopeNotes.statement: power = (energy transferred)/(time) [P = E/t] and power = (work done)/(time) [P = W/t]
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only these two relationships and their direct rearrangements (E = Pt, W = Pt, t = E/P) appear. No efficiency calculation, no power = force x velocity and no gravitational potential energy calculation is used, because 4.1.1.4 defines power only as energy transferred or work done divided by time. In the motor and crane comparisons the work done is stated to be equal rather than calculated from force and distance.

concepts.definition: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred, or the rate at which work is done. It is not a quantity of energy: it says how many joules are transferred each second, so a power value always needs both an energy and a time.
The watt is the unit of power, symbol W. An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt, so 1 W is 1 J/s.
The energy transferred, symbol E, is measured in joules, J. Divided by the time in seconds it gives the power: power = (energy transferred)/(time), [P = E/t].

Work done, symbol W, is measured in joules, J, because doing work is one way of transferring energy. Divided by the time it gives the power: power = (work done)/(time), [P = W/t]. The letter W is also the symbol for the watt; in P = W/t it stands for the work done.
The time, symbol t, is measured in seconds, s. A time given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds before it is used in P = E/t or P = W/t.

Two machines that transfer the same energy, for example two electric motors lifting the same weight through the same height, differ in power only through the time taken. The one that finishes sooner has the greater power.

misconceptions.question: Does a more powerful device always transfer more energy?
misconceptions.correct: A more powerful device transfers energy at a greater rate, that is more joules every second. Over a whole job it may transfer the same total energy as a weaker device, or even less.
misconceptions.misconception: Power just means how much energy something transfers, so the bigger the energy the bigger the power.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'powerful' means big or strong, and both energy and power are introduced with the word 'transfer'. The division by time is easy to drop.
misconceptions.correction: Read the definition as a rate: power = (energy transferred)/(time). Two values are always needed. 1000 J in 1 s is a power of 1000 W; the same 1000 J spread over 100 s is only 10 W.

misconceptions.question: In P = E/t, is the energy transferred found by dividing power by time?
misconceptions.correct: Rearranging P = E/t gives E = Pt, so the energy transferred is the power multiplied by the time.
misconceptions.misconception: E = P/t, or power is energy multiplied by time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students rearrange by pattern-matching rather than by operation, moving whichever symbol they want to the front while leaving the division sign where it was.
misconceptions.correction: Multiply both sides of P = E/t by t to get Pt = E. Check with units: watts multiplied by seconds gives joules, watts divided by seconds does not.

misconceptions.question: Is the joule the unit of power?
misconceptions.correct: Power is measured in watts, W. The joule, J, is the unit of energy transferred and of work done.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy is measured in watts and power in joules, or the two units are interchangeable.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both units appear together in the same equation, and labels such as '2000 W kettle' and 'joules of energy' are met at different times, so the pairing is never fixed.
misconceptions.correction: Fix the pairing from the specification: power, P, in watts, W; energy transferred, E, in joules, J. The watt already contains 'per second'.

misconceptions.question: Is 1 joule the same as 1 watt?
misconceptions.correct: An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt. A joule on its own is not a watt.
misconceptions.misconception: 1 J = 1 W, so the two units can be swapped freely, and larger multiples can be used just as loosely.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words 'per second' are dropped when the relationship is memorised, leaving what looks like a plain equality between two units.
misconceptions.correction: Always say the full statement: one joule per second equals one watt. Writing 1 W = 1 J/s keeps the time in view, and keeps 1 W distinct from 1 kW.

misconceptions.question: Can a time given in minutes be put straight into P = E/t?
misconceptions.correct: No. Time in these equations is in seconds, so 2 minutes must be entered as 120 s.
misconceptions.misconception: Seconds and minutes can be swapped freely, so a factor of 60 can be applied without changing the answer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is remembered as a rule for numbers rather than for quantities, and the unit line 'time, t, in seconds, s' is treated as background information.
misconceptions.correction: Convert first, then substitute: multiply minutes by 60 and hours by 3600. A power that comes out 60 times too big is the signature of this slip.

misconceptions.question: If one motor lifts the same load in half the time, has it done more work?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both motors do the same work on the load, because the weight and the height are the same. The faster motor does that work in less time, so its power is greater.
misconceptions.misconception: The faster machine must have done more work, or transferred more energy, to the load.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Speed is read as effort, so a machine that finishes sooner is assumed to have put more in, and work done and power are not held apart.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two quantities: the work done is fixed by the load and the height, while the power depends on how long that work takes.

misconceptions.question: Is power the time taken divided by the energy transferred?
misconceptions.correct: No, power is the energy transferred divided by the time: P = E/t.
misconceptions.misconception: P = t/E, so a longer time gives a bigger power.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The student remembers that power involves an energy and a time but not their order, and 'it takes longer, so more power' matches the everyday idea that hard jobs need power.
misconceptions.correction: Think in joules per second: the energy goes on top. A device that takes longer to transfer the same energy is less powerful, not more.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of work done?
misconceptions.correct: Work done, W, is measured in joules, J, the same unit as energy transferred, because doing work is a way of transferring energy.
misconceptions.misconception: Work done is measured in newtons, or in watts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Work is introduced through force multiplied by distance, so the newton stays attached to it, and the shared symbol W pulls students towards watts.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states work done, W, in joules, J. Newtons measure force; watts measure power.

misconceptions.question: If a job takes twice as long, what happens to the power?
misconceptions.correct: For the same energy transferred, doubling the time halves the power, because the time is in the denominator of P = E/t.
misconceptions.misconception: Doubling the time doubles the power, since both quantities appear in the same equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any pair of quantities in one equation is assumed to rise together, and the difference between a numerator and a denominator is not checked.
misconceptions.correction: Test with numbers: 600 J in 10 s is 60 W, but 600 J in 20 s is only 30 W.

misconceptions.question: Does 'more powerful' just mean a motor can lift a heavier load?
misconceptions.correct: Power compares rates of energy transfer. Two motors lifting the same weight through the same height differ in power only because one takes less time.
misconceptions.misconception: Power is about how heavy a load a machine can move, or how big a force it exerts, not about how quickly it works.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Advertising uses 'powerful' for strength, and in most questions the loads differ, so weight rather than time is read as the deciding factor.
misconceptions.correction: Hold the load and the height fixed, as the specification example does, and the only difference left is the time taken.

misconceptions.question: In the equation P = W/t, what does W stand for?
misconceptions.correct: W stands for the work done, in joules. The same letter is used for the watt, but in this equation it is the work done.
misconceptions.misconception: W in P = W/t means watts, so the equation reads power equals watts divided by time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol for the unit of power and the symbol for work done are the same letter, and students match letters to units before checking which quantity is meant.
misconceptions.correction: Read the specification pairing: work done, W, in joules, J. A unit never appears as a quantity on the right-hand side of an equation.

mcqs.stem: Which statement gives the definition of power?

options.text: The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done
options.rationale: This is the definition in the specification: power is a rate, so an energy and a time are both involved.

options.text: The total amount of energy that a device transfers
options.rationale: Dropping the time from the definition turns power into a quantity of energy rather than a rate.

options.text: The time that an energy transfer takes to finish
options.rationale: Chosen by students who recall that time appears in the definition but give it the wrong role.

options.text: The force that a machine uses to shift a load
options.rationale: Confuses power with force, because 'powerful' in everyday use suggests strength rather than a rate.

mcqs.stem: Which word equation for power is given in the specification?

options.text: power = energy transferred x time
options.rationale: Reads as though a longer time gives a greater power, the direct-proportion error; energy multiplied by time gives an energy, not a power.

options.text: power = time taken / energy transferred
options.rationale: The inverted equation, chosen by students who recall both quantities but not their order.

options.text: power = energy transferred / the time
options.rationale: Matches power = (energy transferred)/(time), written in symbols as P = E/t.

options.text: power = the work done x time taken
options.rationale: Uses the work-done version of the equation but multiplies instead of dividing, the standard rearrangement error.

mcqs.stem: In the equation P = E/t, which units should be used for E and for t?

options.text: energy in newtons and time in seconds
options.rationale: The newton is a unit of force; it gets attached to energy through the force x distance route to work.

options.text: energy in joules and time in seconds
options.rationale: The specification gives energy transferred, E, in joules, J, and time, t, in seconds, s.

options.text: energy in watts and time in seconds
options.rationale: Swaps the units of the two quantities: the watt belongs to P, not to E.

options.text: energy in joules and time in hours
options.rationale: Time must be in seconds; hours shrink the denominator, so the power comes out 3600 times too large.

mcqs.stem: An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of:

options.text: 1 joule
options.rationale: Keeps the energy unit for a power, treating the joule as if it measured how fast energy is transferred.

options.text: 60 watts
options.rationale: Comes from converting 'per second' into 'per minute', a time-unit slip rather than a reading of the definition.

options.text: 1 kilowatt
options.rationale: Right unit family, wrong size: the equality is with one watt, not with one thousand watts.

options.text: 1 watt
options.rationale: This is the statement in the specification: 1 joule per second is a power of 1 watt.

mcqs.stem: A kettle transfers 360 000 J of energy in 180 s. What is its power?

options.rationale: The result of dividing time by energy, 180 / 360 000, so the equation has been inverted.
Comes from using 3 minutes instead of 180 s, giving an answer 60 times too large.
P = E/t = 360 000 / 180 = 2000 W, that is 2000 joules transferred every second.
Energy multiplied by time instead of divided by it, the classic rearrangement error.

mcqs.stem: A crane does 90 000 J of work in 30 s. What is the power of the crane?

options.rationale: P = W/t = 90 000 / 30 = 3000 W, using power = (work done)/(time).
Quotes the work done as if it were the power, ignoring the division by time.
Comes from dividing by 1800 s, treating the 30 s as though it were 30 minutes.
Work done multiplied by the time rather than divided by it.

mcqs.stem: Two electric motors lift identical loads through the same height. Motor A takes 4 s and motor B takes 10 s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Motor A is more powerful, because it must have done extra work on the load
options.rationale: The work done is the same for both motors, because the loads and heights are identical; only the time differs.

options.text: Motor B is more powerful, because it keeps working for a longer time
options.rationale: Treats time as though it multiplied the power instead of dividing it.

options.text: Both motors have equal power, because the work done on the load is equal
options.rationale: Equal work does not mean equal power, because the two motors take different times.

options.text: Motor A is more powerful, because it does the same work in a shorter time
options.rationale: Equal loads through equal heights means equal work done, so the shorter time gives the greater power.

mcqs.stem: A 1500 W heater is switched on for 300 s. How much energy does it transfer?

options.rationale: Student rearranges wrongly to E = P/t and computes 1500 divided by 30 (misreading 300 s), giving 50 J.
Rearranging P = E/t gives E = Pt = 1500 x 300 = 450 000 J.

options.text: 5 J
options.rationale: Uses E = P/t, dividing 1500 by 300 rather than multiplying.
Uses t/P, 300 divided by 1500, inverting the relationship completely.

mcqs.stem: The specification gives the equation P = W/t. What does W stand for in this equation?

options.text: the power in watts, as W is its unit
options.rationale: Reads the symbol as the unit of power; a unit cannot be a quantity on the right of the equation.

options.text: the work done, measured in newtons
options.rationale: Right quantity, wrong unit: newtons measure force, not the work that a force does.

options.text: the weight lifted, in newtons
options.rationale: Confuses the work done with the weight lifted, which is a force rather than an energy transfer.

options.text: the work done, measured in joules
options.rationale: The specification pairs work done, W, with joules, J; power is the work done divided by the time.

mcqs.stem: A motor transfers 15 000 J of energy in 2 minutes. What is its power?

options.rationale: Divides by 2 rather than by 120 s, the standard failure to convert minutes into seconds.
2 minutes is 120 s, so P = E/t = 15 000 / 120 = 125 W.
Divides the time by the energy, 120 / 15 000, inverting the equation.
Multiplies 15 000 by 120 instead of dividing, giving an impossible power for a small motor.

mcqs.stem: A lamp transfers 500 J of energy while a pump does 500 J of work. Which statement about the units is correct?

options.text: Both are in joules, because doing work is a way of transferring energy
options.rationale: The specification gives energy transferred, E, in joules, and work done, W, in joules.

options.text: Work done is in newtons, so the two quantities cannot be compared
options.rationale: Carries the newton over from force x distance, when the product of the two is in joules.

options.text: Energy transferred is in watts, so only the work is in joules
options.rationale: Gives energy the unit of power; the watt already includes 'per second'.

options.text: Energy transferred is in joules but work done is in watts
options.rationale: Reads the W of work done as the watt; in P = W/t, W is the work done, in joules.

mcqs.stem: Two cranes lift the same load to the same height. Crane X takes 20 s and crane Y takes 50 s. Which quantity is different for the two cranes?

options.text: the work done on the load
options.rationale: The work done depends on the load and the height, both of which are the same here.

options.text: the energy passed to the load
options.rationale: Assumes the faster crane must pass more energy to the load, when it passes the same energy sooner.

options.text: the power of the two cranes
options.rationale: The same work done in different times means different rates of transfer, so the powers differ.

options.text: the weight of the loads lifted
options.rationale: The loads are stated to be the same; power is being read as strength rather than as a rate.
